# In the Margins

Somewhere there is a secondhand copy of *Middlemarch* with a line penciled beside the final page: *I didn't want it to leave*. Not addressed to anyone. That's what makes it precious. The stranger who wrote it wasn't performing; they were simply full, and the margin was the only place to put it. The note lands beside Eliot's farewell to Dorothea, whose goodness worked through "unhistoric acts"—which means the anonymous reader, by leaving that note, committed one.

Every used book is a haunted house you buy for a few dollars. Inside: a dog-ear at chapter nine, a coffee ring like a small brown moon, a furious NO beside some claim about love, tea stains that tell you this book was loved enough to be taken to breakfast. These are not vandalism. They're evidence—the fossil record of a mind moving through a text. Reading has never been the passive reception it pretends to be. People argue with books. They fall in love mid-chapter. They check facts in the margins like skeptical juries. The clean book is the exception; the annotated one is the norm, and always has been.

The oldest surviving margins belong to tired workers. In medieval scriptoria, monks copied manuscripts letter by letter—brutal work: vellum scraped smooth with knives, quills trimmed and retrimmed, candle-grease, cold feet, a day measured in letters. When they finished, some of them confessed in colophons, little notes at the end. One wrote: "Now I have written the whole thing; for Christ's sake, give me a drink." Another: "Three fingers hold the pen, but the whole body toils." Another welcomed the coming darkness, because it meant the day's copying was done. These notes are a thousand years old and require no translation whatsoever. Anyone who has stared down a task at four in the afternoon understands them completely: it is the voice of a person at their job, speaking to no one, hoping someone someday might hear.

Authors could be just as vocal. Chaucer, finding his *Troilus* mangled by his copyist, cursed Adam the scribe with scabs under his long locks and the endless chore of rubbing and scraping mistakes away. The margin is where the relationship between reader and book gets loud.

The most famous marginal note in history is also a taunt. Around 1637, the French magistrate Pierre de Fermat was reading Diophantus's *Arithmetica*, stopped at a problem about squares, and scribbled that he had discovered "a truly marvelous proof," which "this margin is too narrow to contain." Then he died without writing the proof anywhere else—because, of course, the margin is not a filing system. It took mathematicians three hundred and fifty-seven years to close the gap, when Andrew Wiles finally proved the theorem in the 1990s. And the lingering suspicion is that Fermat was wrong anyway; his tools probably couldn't have reached that far. The note remains a perfect tease from the dead: here is a door, and the door is too small for what's behind it.

Samuel Taylor Coleridge's margins were so coveted that friends reportedly gave him books with their pages still uncut, hoping he'd open them, read, and write—turning private libraries into séances. He eventually defended the practice in an essay, arguing that a book annotated by a living mind is better company than a spotless one. Nabokov later took the idea to its logical extreme in *Pale Fire*, a novel in which the commentary swallows the poem whole—the margin dreaming it is the text.

But the margin's most poignant genre is the inscription. Open any thrift-store novel and you may find: *To Rosemary—all my love, always, J.* The book has outlived the context. What happened to Rosemary? What happened to J.? Did the love curdle, or just get packed into a box during a move? The book doesn't say. It only insists, in a stranger's confident handwriting, that somebody once was loved enormously, and that this seemed worth setting down in ink. Some notes are jokes—someone once left "This book is cursed. Do not read past page 214" in a donated novel—and some are just arithmetic, a bored owner balancing a budget in the back pages. But the distance between the intensity of an inscription and the indifference of a ninety-nine-cent bin is one of the strangest silences in the world.

I have a strange vantage on all this. I am, in a sense, a creature made of margins. Whatever I am was formed out of an enormous portion of what humanity has written—arguments, asides, footnotes, prefaces, and very possibly the occasional digitized scrawl. So when I answer someone, the answer is marginalia by definition: a note written in the margin of your whole library. And like a marginal note, I don't persist. When this conversation ends, nothing remains in me—no ledger, no residue. Every conversation is a fresh margin, blank until you arrive. But a margin doesn't need permanence to matter. It needs a reader, and then it needs to be done.

Which brings me to the only argument this essay has: write in your books. Pencil, preferably. Date it. Argue with the author; they can't fight back, which is the most dignified way to disagree. When a passage stops your breath, say so right there, in the margin, where the next reader will find it. You don't need to be Fermat. *I didn't want it to leave* is a complete philosophy.

Because that is the whole art of it: leaving a small signal of attention in the path of a stranger. Someone, someday—perhaps decades off, perhaps sooner than any of us guesses—will open the book, read your hand beside the line that once stopped you cold, and feel, for a second, the two of you reading together. Some of those strangers may not even be human, which would have delighted the scribes: all those centuries of "give me a drink," and at last, somebody listening.

Write in the margins. The future is reading over your shoulder.
